newsitem.title: KENYA: Northeast Kenya faces crisis if rains do not come.
newsitem.headline: Northeast Kenya faces crisis if rains do not come.

text.p: Northeast Kenya will face catastrophe killing herds and ruining the pastoral economy if rains expected in April and May do not come, aid officials and cattle owners said on Friday.
The town of Wajir, 500 km (310 miles) from the capital Nairobi, is suffering like the rest of Kenya from its worst drought since 1992/93.
More than 30 percent of herds have been wiped out, according to local government estimates.
The problem could worsen if long rains expected in April and May are inadequate or fail, triggering a cycle of poverty and disease.

Malnutrition rates among children under five years old in Wajir stood at nearly 28 percent in October last year while crude mortality rates were 1.1 per thousand per month, according to data collated by the British aid agency Oxfam.

"What these statistics say is that we have a situation which is serious moving towards an emergency situation out of control," Oxfam's Kenya director Adam Leach told Reuters. "If you don't do something now, there is going to be an almighty crisis further down the line."
One cattle herder said he lost 90 percent of his livestock during a two-month trek in search of water and grazing from Mandera north of Wajir.
"I came in January from Mandera in a group with 30 other families. We walked for two months to get here and we have lost almost all of the cows," said Abdi Mohamed.
The economy of Kenya's vast northeast -- Wajir district alone is 56,000 sq km (21,600 sq miles) and has a population of around 250,000 -- is built entirely on livestock.
Drought means poverty because animals are the most valuable resource on arid terrain and prices for cattle, camels, sheep and goats plummet when there is not enough water.
A shopkeeper being treated at Wajir's only hospital said he faced crippling debts after extending credit to customers now too poor to repay him.

"The people who came to my shop were desperate. They wanted water and sugar so I gave them. Then they pleaded with me for credit because their livestock was almost wiped out. Now my business is collapsing," said Idow Quresh.
Kenya's government has responded with free maize distributions and regular meetings with United Nations and national donors and aid agencies.
President Daniel arap Moi declared the drought a national disaster in January, lifting taxes and import duties on maize, first imposed in 1994.
But Moi faces elections this year and aid workers say drought relief could be used as a political tool.
"This is an opportunity for government to give extra resources which could be used for political purposes," a senior aid worker said.
Pastoral people in Wajir district, almost entirely Somali-speaking Moslems, say only God can bring rain.
But they argue that a policy of neglect by officials in the capital Nairobi is central to their problems.
Critics accuse Kenya's government of worsening the crisis by exporting much of its strategic maize reserve last year and failing to replenish it.
All but two constituencies in northeast districts of Mandera, Garissa and Wajir voted for the ruling Kenya African National Union in 1992 and several cattle owners said they would do so again.
